one_liner: Presortedness-detecting merge layer over pdqsort; beats std::sort/std::stable_sort when input has long sorted runs.
what_it_does: Vergesort is not a standalone sorting algorithm but a thin layer that scans a range for sorted or reverse-sorted runs longer than n/log n, merges those runs, and falls back to another sorter (bundled pdqsort for random-access iterators, a median-of-9 quicksort for bidirectional iterators) for the rest. The API is two free functions with the same two- or three-argument shape as std::sort: `vergesort::vergesort(first, last)` and `vergesort::vergesort(first, last, compare)`. It ships as a single self-contained `vergesort.h`, plus a modular version under `include/vergesort/` for reading the implementation.
how_it_is_fast: The random-access overload jumps n/log n elements at a time instead of scanning one by one, so it can decide a run is not 'big enough' after O(log n) comparisons and bail out to pdqsort almost immediately on random data. When a big-enough run is found it records its bounds (reversing descending runs) instead of sorting it, and once the whole range is scanned it k-way-merges the collected runs with std::inplace_merge. The bidirectional overload lacks the jump-scan (it must walk linearly) and falls back to plain median-of-9 quicksort instead of pdqsort, which is why the README documents it as slower and O(n^2) worst case.
when_to_use: Large std::vector-like collections of comparison-sortable types that frequently contain long sorted or reverse-sorted runs (>= n/log n), e.g. pipe-organ, push-front/push-middle, or nearly-sorted-log patterns
You already use (or would use) pdqsort/std::sort and want a near-zero-cost presortedness check layered on top, since the fallback triggers in O(log n) comparisons on random data
std::list or other bidirectional-only sequences where std::list::sort could benefit from run detection, if you can accept the bidirectional overload's O(n^2) worst case
Header-only, dependency-free, C++03-compatible environments where vendoring one file is preferable to adding a library
One-shot throughput sorts of 10^6+ elements where instability is acceptable
when_not_to_use: You need a stable sort: vergesort reverses descending runs in place, which makes it unstable even though its fallback (pdqsort) is also unstable
Data is uniformly random/shuffled with no long runs: the win over calling pdqsort directly is essentially just avoiding vergesort's own scan overhead, not a speedup over pdqsort
Bidirectional-iterator use (e.g. std::list) where adversarial input could hit the documented O(n^2) worst case from the median-of-9 quicksort fallback
Workloads resembling the README's 'Alternating' pattern, where the shown benchmark has vergesort slower than std::stable_sort (~307 vs ~185 cycles/element)

Serious/production integer-sorting workloads chasing maximum speed: the repo's own maintainer calls this standalone header 'more of a demonstrator' and points to the same author's cpp-sort library (cppsort::verge_sort) as the tuned, faster version

integration.dependencies: none — bundles its own pdqsort, insertion sort, iter_sort3, log2 and quicksort helper headers; standard library only
integration.min_toolchain: C++03 for the standalone header (README: 'Everything should work with even C++03'); benchmarks were built with MinGW g++ 6.1.0 -std=c++1z -O2 -march=native
integration.platforms: any (portable C++, no platform-specific intrinsics in the header); benchmark hardware itself is undocumented
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — same call signature as std::sort (iterators, optional comparator), but it is unstable, and the bidirectional overload for std::list-like containers is a separate, slower code path with an O(n^2) worst case

gotchas: Unstable by design: it uses std::reverse on descending runs before merging, which discards relative order of equal elements even when the fallback sorter is stable

A real 2020 bug (issue #13) had the standalone header's random-access overload silently misnamed/uncalled, so it fell through to the much slower bidirectional path — fixed after report, but shows the single-header demo has drifted out of sync with cpp-sort's verge_sort before
The 'big enough' run threshold is a fixed n/log n heuristic with no tuning parameter; the author notes it is sometimes suboptimal versus always falling back

The bidirectional-iterator variant cannot use the jump-scan optimization and falls back to a plain median-of-9 quicksort, giving it O(n^2) worst case (vs O(n log n) worst case for the random-access version)
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick vergesort over pdqsort when your data regularly contains long sorted/reverse-sorted runs (pipe-organ, push-front/middle, nearly-sorted-log shapes) and unstable output is acceptable — pdqsort alone is the safer default for uniformly random data since vergesort only adds a fast-fail scan there. Prefer ska_sort or Highway's vqsort instead when the win you need comes from key-type specialization (integer radix) or SIMD partitioning rather than run detection, since vergesort's fallbacks.md shows it still beats raw ska_sort on presorted patterns but the 'vergesort killer' pattern narrows that gap (139 vs 127 cycles/element).
verified_claims_summary: Chart-derived cycles-per-element numbers (std::vector<int>, 10^6 elements, MinGW g++ 6.1.0 -std=c++1z -O2 -march=native, libstdc++, no CPU model stated) show vergesort's pdqsort-backed random-access version beating libstdc++ std::sort on every distribution charted (e.g. shuffled ~365 vs ~713, pipe organ ~22 vs ~885, push front ~15 vs ~858) and beating std::stable_sort on most patterns, but losing to std::stable_sort on the 'Alternating' pattern (~307 vs ~185).
status_note: Actively maintained (pushed 2025-11-07) and MIT-licensed, but the author has stated on the issue tracker that this standalone single-header version is 'more of a demonstrator' favoring small code size and C++03 backward compatibility over raw speed — the actively tuned, faster implementation is cppsort::verge_sort in the same author's cpp-sort project.
